title.narrative: LEADING FROM THE SOUTH PII (2021-2025)

description.narrative: Leading from the South is an initiative conceptualized for Women’s Funds working on women’s rights issues and gender equality within Africa and the MENA region, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean and globally. The fund is managed by four prominent Women’s Funds: Fondo de Mujeres del Sur –FMS- (Latin America and the Caribbean), the African Women’s Development Fund –AWDF- (Africa and the MENA Region), the South Asia Women Fund –SAWF- (Asia) and the International Indigenous Women’s Forum –FIMI- (Global); supported by the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands. The aim of the initiative is to resource and support Women’s Rights Organisations (Small grassroots, Intermediate, Large, and consortium/Networks) in the Global South in their advocacy work to achieve gender equality. Following the successful implementation of Leading from the South (LFS) PI: Resources for Women’s Rights Advocacy for Full Equality (2017-2020) by the consortium, the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) has made available €80 million for phase II of the LFS (2021-2025) to strengthen the lobby and advocacy capacity of Southern women’s organisations, movements and networks at regional, national and grassroots level. Outcomes from LFS phase I provided a justification for the MFA to consider a phase II. African Women’s Development Fund (AWDF) is a Pan-African grant-making organisation that funds local, national, and regional autonomous women’s rights organisations in Africa and the Middle East, that are working towards the promotion and realisation African Women’s Rights. Since the beginning of its operation in 2001, AWDF has awarded grants and provided technical support to over 1,400 women’s organisations in 43 out of the 54 countries in Africa. AWDF mobilises financial, human and material resources to support local, national, and regional initiatives for transformation led by women in Africa and the Middle East towards achieving its vision.

Resource Women's Rights Organisations working on women's rights activism, lobbying and advocacy for gender equality in the Global South, to achieve maximum results for women's and girls human rights in their regions.

The target groups of the Leading from the South initiative are grassroots, small, medium, and large women´s rights organisations, whose core mandate is to work towards the achievement of gender equity and the full realisation of the rights of women, girls and other marginalised groups in the Global South.

Outcome 3: Improved laws and policies that advance womens' and girls' rights

description.narrative: Number of laws, policies and strategies blocked, adopted or improved

title.narrative: BASELINE DATA ASSESSMENT LEADING FROM THE SOUTH PROJECT

WRGE indicator 2.1. # of laws, policies and strategies blocked, adopted or improved to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in public, private and civic sphere. (link SCS2)

description.narrative: number of laws, policies and strategies blocked, adopted, or improved

comment.narrative: Grantees' projects contributed to a change in 36 laws and policies by the end of LFS PI implementation. Details of this information can be found in the final end of project report LFS PI and Baseline report

AWDF anticipates that selected CSOs' Lobbying and Advocacy activities will influence, governments, private sector and societal groups to change their laws and policies, to support sustainability and gender inclusiveness over the five-year period.

Our funded partners worked to influence government agencies and traditional authorities to change policies and laws to promote the rights of women, girls, and gender-diverse persons and to create a safe and inclusive environment. They influenced the adoption and improvement of laws at local and national levels. Since project inception, our grantee partners in Kenya, Algeria, Burundi, Cameroon, Nigeria and Yemen have engaged with and lobbied duty-bearers, and initiated processes to adopt new laws and improve 7 existing laws and policies to promote women's and girls’ rights and the rights of gender-diverse persons in their countries and communities. In Kenya, the Siaya Widows Protection Act, 2025, formally recognised widows as rights holders. Ritual cleansing and property dispossession are prohibited. Advocacy anchored by systematic documentation of widow testimonies, translated into a charter, and carried across an election cycle. Under this indicator, the variance is driven largely by the same shifts in operating context that affect partners’ broader advocacy work. Legislative and policy processes targeted by partners in different countries were deprioritised as governments contended with political instability, including coups and transitions that disrupted parliamentary sessions and policy timelines altogether. Where processes did continue, they were met with organised resistance from anti-rights and anti-gender actors, who have grown more effective at blocking or diluting progressive reforms on gender-based violence and gender justice in general, often reframing them as threats to cultural or religious values. Restrictive NGO laws and heightened surveillance further limited partners' ability to engage decision-makers directly or sustain the kind of visible, coordinated advocacy that law and policy change typically requires. As a result, several planned interventions shifted from active reform pushes to defensive advocacy, protecting existing legal gains from rollback rather than advancing new ones. The actual achievements, therefore, represent meaningful progress secured against a considerably more constrained legislative environment. Looking ahead, we are supporting partners to build longer-term, more resilient policy advocacy strategies suited to this closing space.

title.narrative: Outcome 2: The enabling environment is strengthened to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in the public, private, and civic spheres

title.narrative: BASELINE DATA ASSESSMENT LEADING FROM THE SOUTH PROJECT

2.1 - # of times that CSOs succeed in creating space for CSO demands and positions on violence against women and girls through agenda setting, influencing the debate, and/or movement-building (link SCS3)

description.narrative: Number of times CSOs succeed in creating space for CSOs demands and positions

comment.narrative: During phase one all supported Women's Rights Organisations engaged in advocacy. And at least 36 of the supported WROs successfully created various spaces for their demands and positions to be heard. This contributed to the improvement of 36 laws. For more qualitative information, please refer to the Baseline report and End of project reporting (Phase 1).

AWDF anticipates that targeted women's rights organisations and CSOs will play a transformative role in decision-making processes in their constituencies through agenda setting, influencing debate, and/or successfully creating space to engage with key stakeholders and duty-bearers.

Despite shrinking civic space and the challenges faced by feminist and women’s rights organisations, our grantee partners created spaces to engage with their communities and to advocate for advancing the agenda for women's and girls' rights. They leveraged the anchoring power of their networks and alliances to ensure greater impact. As at the time of reporting, our funded partners in Ghana, Mozambique, Algeria, Kenya, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe created spaces for their demands and positions to be heard at least 60 times. This was done by implementing advocacy and reflection forums, developing formal and informal frameworks to position civil society organisations' needs and highlighting and demanding relevant changes that promote gender justice. They also used social media to ignite different conversations and debates online. Their engagements have contributed to commitments from duty bearers. The variance recorded under this indicator reflects a marked deterioration in the operating context since the target was originally set in 2021, rather than a failure of partner strategy or effort. Civic space has closed rapidly across most of the countries in which we work. Several have experienced coups and the accompanying suspension or restriction of democratic processes, curtailing the political and institutional spaces through which CSOs would ordinarily advance advocacy on VAWG. At the same time, anti-rights and anti-gender movements have grown more organised and vocal, actively contesting and pushing back against gains on gender equality and women's rights, and in many contexts dominating public discourse and policy debate. This has been compounded by increasingly close surveillance of NGO activity and the introduction or enforcement of restrictive laws governing civil society operations, both of which have constrained partners' ability to organise, mobilise, and engage decision-makers openly. Taken together, these shifts have narrowed the political opportunity structures on which this indicator depends. Partners have had to redirect significant energy toward protecting existing space and ensuring their own safety and operational continuity, rather than expanding into new advocacy terrain. Despite this, the actual instances achieved represent meaningful wins secured under considerably more hostile conditions than anticipated at the inception stage. Looking ahead, we will work with partners to adapt advocacy strategies to closing civic space, including lower-profile and coalition-based approaches and will improve target-setting for similar indicators to better reflect current contextual realities under LFS III.

AWDF aims to strengthen the lobbying and advocacy capacity of three targeted grassroots, national and regional feminist/minority-led organisations and CSOs through funding, capacity building, and cross-learning opportunities to effectively implement gender-sensitive advocacy strategies and affect policy change and policy implementation.

1 women with disability-led organisation, 1 indigenous women-led organisation, 2 female sex-worker-led organisations, and 1 refugee women-led that received grants under LFS (both in Africa) reported an increased capacity to lobby and advocate, through the contribution of AWDF’s institutional strengthening and financial (grant) support. AWDF's USD 9,000 capacity support grant meant organisations could conduct capacity-building training for their staff, contributing to their ability to deliver on their mandates and implement advocacy strategies. We exceeded this target.

AWDF aims to strengthen the lobbying and advocacy capacity of fourteen targeted grassroots, national and regional feminist/minority-led organisations and CSOs through funding, capacity building, and cross-learning opportunities to effectively implement gender-sensitive advocacy strategies and affect policy change and policy implementation.

Eight organisations in Africa and the Middle East, including two disability-led organisations, one indigenous women-led organisation, one domestic-worker-led organisation, one LBTQI-led organisation, and three sex-worker-led organisations, reported increased ability to lobby and advocate. The organisations cited that AWDF’s support contributed to strengthening their ability to lobby and advocate. The variance represents a deliberate shift to provide fewer, larger multi-year grants in years 3 and 4, enabling partners to deepen and expand their work and to counter anti-rights and anti-gender organising by strengthening the voice and leadership of gender-diverse activists and their organisations. This builds on the approach adopted the year prior, with enhanced proactive strategising and collective responses to legal reforms that seek to police sexual and gender identities and roll back progressive laws and policies. Most resources in 2025 went toward the Beijing+30 process, allowing us to fully leverage the significant advocacy opportunities it presented, culminating at CSW69 in March 2025.

AWDF aims to strengthen the lobbying and advocacy capacity of fourteen targeted grassroots, national and regional feminist/minority-led organisations and CSOs through funding, capacity building, and cross-learning opportunities to effectively implement gender-sensitive advocacy strategies and affect policy change and policy implementation.

In 2025, no new organisation was counted as having increased capacity, as most partners were implementing multi-year grants. However, all the organisations that responded to the annual progress survey reported an increase in their ability to lobby and advocate. The organisations cited that AWDF’s support strengthened their ability. The variance under this indicator reflects two main factors. First, a deliberate shift to provide fewer, larger multi-year grants in years 3 and 4, enabling partners to deepen and expand their work and to counter anti-rights and anti-gender organising by strengthening the voice and leadership of gender-diverse activists and their organisations. This builds on the approach adopted the year prior, with enhanced proactive strategising and collective responses to legal reforms that seek to police sexual and gender identities and roll back progressive laws and policies. Most resources in 2025 went toward the Beijing+30 process, allowing us to fully leverage the significant advocacy opportunities it presented, culminating at CSW69 in March 2025. Second, our reporting relies on an annual partner survey. Most partners active in 2025 were implementing multi-year grants and had already been counted under an earlier implementation year, so they could not be included again under the 'no double-counting' requirement. Of the 54 partners who responded to this year's survey, all had been reported under this output in a previous year, and have progressively strengthened their capacity since. The quantitative variance, therefore, does not signify an underachievement of impact on the ground: per our evaluation report, 80% of grantee partners strengthened their MEL systems over the implementation period, and 70% reported strengthened fundraising capacity, among other gains. In practice, AWDF supported far more organisations in 2025 than the actual figure shows, but we can only report in line with MFA requirements. Looking ahead, we are strengthening our monitoring and evaluation systems to improve target-setting and the capture of results.
